units.title: Unit 37 — Money
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 78–79 (PDF pages 82–83).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
learningObjectives: Use conventional verbs for spending, saving, wasting, exchanging and donating money, including appropriate prepositions.
Describe prices as high or low, soaring or falling, and distinguish fair prices from unusually low or absurd ones.
Discuss income, financial shortages, withdrawals, fundraising and money invested in a business.
Recognise informal and evaluative expressions such as throw money around, going cheap and make a small fortune.

items.example: We spend money on transport instead of driving our own car.
items.note: Spend money on names the purpose of an expenditure; spend money in something is not the usual pattern.

items.example: She saves money every month for an emergency fund.
items.note: Save means keep money for later rather than spending it now; it can also mean reducing a cost.

items.example: We wasted money on software that no one used.
items.note: Waste implies that the expense had little or no useful result; follow it with on for the purchase or activity.

items.pt: esbanjar dinheiro; dissipar uma quantia de dinheiro
items.example: The character squandered money from his inheritance on luxury trips.
items.note: Squander is strongly critical and typically suggests wasting a substantial amount of money.

items.pt: trocar dinheiro por outra moeda; fazer câmbio
items.example: Travellers can change money at the exchange desk before leaving.
items.note: Change money refers to exchanging currencies, not simply receiving change after paying.

items.pt: gastar dinheiro de modo ostensivo e irresponsável
items.example: He was throwing money around to impress his new colleagues.
items.note: Informal and disapproving; suggests careless, showy spending on unnecessary things.

items.pt: tentar resolver um problema gastando muito dinheiro
items.example: Management cannot fix a weak design simply by throwing money at the problem.
items.note: Throw money at suggests spending large sums on a problem, often without an effective plan.

items.pt: doar dinheiro para uma instituição beneficente; fazer doações
items.example: The club donates money to charity after its annual event.
items.note: Donate is more formal than give and commonly takes to for the receiving organisation.

items.example: High prices forced the family to postpone their holiday.
items.note: High and low are the usual adjectives for prices; tall prices is incorrect.

items.example: The supermarket attracted customers with consistently low prices.
items.note: Low is the standard opposite of high when talking about prices.

items.pt: preços extremamente baixos; preços no mínimo possível
items.example: The shop sold last season's jackets at rock-bottom prices.
items.note: An emphatic expression for exceptionally low prices, often used in advertising.

items.pt: os preços sobem; aumento dos preços
items.example: Prices go up when demand rises faster than supply.
items.note: Go up is a common informal way to describe increases in prices; prices rise is a more neutral alternative.

items.pt: os preços aumentam; os preços sobem
items.example: Food prices rise when production costs increase.
items.note: Rise is intransitive here; do not say that prices raise without an object.

items.example: Housing prices soared in the fictional coastal town last spring.
items.note: Soar means rise very rapidly or dramatically, not merely increase a little.

items.pt: os preços caem; os preços diminuem
items.example: Fuel prices went down after the holiday season.
items.note: Go down means decrease in this context; it contrasts with prices go up.

items.pt: com preço razoável; vendido por um valor justo
items.example: The restaurant offers reasonably priced meals near the station.
items.note: Describes a price that seems fair rather than especially cheap or expensive.

items.pt: um preço absurdo; um preço inacreditável
items.example: The collector paid a ridiculous price for a damaged poster.
items.note: Depending on the context, ridiculous can criticise an excessively high price or describe an unbelievably low one.

items.pt: o dinheiro está curto; o orçamento está apertado
items.example: Money is tight this month, so we are avoiding unnecessary purchases.
items.note: An informal expression meaning there is little money available to spend.

items.pt: há pouco dinheiro disponível; o dinheiro está escasso
items.example: Money was in short supply during the first year of the project.
items.note: In short supply means insufficiently available; it can be used with goods and resources as well.

items.example: A steady income helped the family plan for the future.
items.note: Steady describes income received regularly or reliably, not necessarily a large amount.

items.example: She earns a good salary as an experienced technician.
items.note: Earn refers to payment for work; a salary usually means a regular amount paid by an employer.

items.example: He hoped to make big money from his new business.
items.note: Informal expression meaning earn or gain a great deal of money.

items.example: The novel's main character becomes seriously rich after selling her company.
items.note: Informal intensifier seriously means extremely in this expression.

items.example: The small company finally started making money after two difficult years.
items.note: Make money can mean earn money or operate profitably; it is not the same as physically printing money.

items.pt: ganhar dinheiro por meio de trabalho
items.example: Students sometimes earn money through weekend jobs.
items.note: Earn highlights receiving payment in return for work or services; make money is broader.

items.word: put money in a bank account
items.pt: depositar dinheiro em uma conta bancária
items.example: He put some money in a bank account for future repairs.
items.note: Put money in an account is an everyday way to describe depositing funds.

items.example: She opened a bank account to receive her salary.
items.note: Account is countable here; bank account names the arrangement in which a bank holds money.

items.pt: fazer um saque; retirar dinheiro da conta
items.example: The customer made a withdrawal before the bank closed.
items.note: Withdrawal is the noun for taking funds from an account; the usual verb is make, not take a withdrawal.

items.example: The association raised money to repair the community centre.
items.note: Raise means obtain funds, often through donors, investors or loans; it does not simply mean increase existing money.

items.pt: fazer um bom negócio; conseguir uma boa oferta
items.example: We got a good deal on a second-hand desk.
items.note: A good deal is a favourable purchase or agreement; it is informal.

items.pt: ser vendido barato; sair por um preço baixo
items.example: The old computer was going cheap because its battery needed replacing.
items.note: Informal expression for something being sold at a low price; go is not literal movement.

items.pt: ganhar uma boa quantia; fazer uma pequena fortuna
items.example: She made a small fortune by selling specialist equipment.
items.note: Despite small, the expression means earning or accumulating a substantial sum.

items.example: Most of our money is tied up in equipment at the moment.
items.note: Money tied up in an asset or business is not freely available to spend.

units.title: Unit 38 — War and peace
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 80–81 (PDF pages 84–85).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Topics: Society and institutions · war and peace
learningObjectives: Describe the start, development and decisive events of an armed conflict using natural military collocations.
Distinguish declaring war, going to war, opening fire and being taken prisoner.
Discuss ceasefires, agreements, peacekeeping and the difference between establishing peace and maintaining it.
Understand literal and figurative uses of battle, fight and war in everyday speech and public discourse.

items.pt: a guerra começa; um conflito armado eclode
items.example: War broke out between the two fictional kingdoms after the border dispute.
items.note: Break out means begin suddenly, especially for a war, fire or disease.

items.pt: entrar para o Exército; alistar-se no Exército
items.example: His grandfather joined the army when he was nineteen.
items.note: Join is the normal verb when someone becomes a member of the armed forces.

items.example: In the historical drama, the government declared war after negotiations failed.
items.note: Declare war is a formal announcement that a state is entering a war.

items.pt: entrar em guerra; ir para a guerra
items.example: Both leaders feared their countries might go to war.
items.note: Go to war usually means begin or become involved in armed conflict, not simply travel somewhere.

items.example: The fictional government sent troops to protect the evacuation route.
items.note: Troops refers to groups of soldiers sent on an operation.

items.example: Fierce fighting continued around the town in the novel.
items.note: Fierce intensifies the violence and severity of the fighting, not its duration.

items.example: The dispute began with minor incidents near the border.
items.note: Minor contrasts with serious or major, and here describes relatively limited events.

items.pt: guerra total; guerra em larga escala
items.example: The novel shows how the dispute developed into all-out war.
items.note: All-out describes a conflict waged on a very large or unrestricted scale.

items.pt: entrar no alcance de tiro; ficar ao alcance das armas
items.example: The patrol turned back before coming within firing range of the fortress.
items.note: Within firing range means close enough to be hit by weapons; it does not necessarily mean shots are fired.

items.example: In the film, the soldiers opened fire after an alarm sounded.
items.note: Open fire means begin shooting, usually with firearms; open is not literal opening.

items.example: Several soldiers were taken prisoner during the fictional battle.
items.note: The passive expression means captured and held, especially in a military context.

items.pt: entrar em ação; iniciar uma operação
items.example: The rescue team went into action immediately after the alert.
items.note: Describes starting to operate, especially in an organised group; it can extend beyond military use.

items.example: The final chapter describes a decisive battle that ended the conflict.
items.note: Decisive means determining the overall result, not simply unusually violent.

items.pt: uma batalha ocorre com violência; uma batalha se intensifica
items.example: A battle raged outside the city for several days.
items.note: Rage describes severe and often prolonged conflict; the collocation is common in accounts of war.

items.pt: travar uma guerra; lutar em uma guerra
items.example: The two countries fought a long war over disputed territory.
items.note: Fight a war treats war as the conflict being waged; fight for peace is a different construction.

items.example: Peacekeeping forces arrived after the parties agreed to a ceasefire.
items.note: Forces here means organised military or security personnel assigned to maintain peace.

items.example: The museum exhibition records the horrors of war through personal accounts.
items.note: A fixed emotive expression for the suffering and destruction caused by war.

items.pt: evitar a guerra; impedir um conflito armado
items.example: Diplomats held emergency meetings in an attempt to avert war.
items.note: Avert means prevent a threatened event before it happens; do not confuse it with end a war already in progress.

items.pt: promover a paz; conseguir estabelecer a paz
items.example: The mediators worked for years to bring about peace.
items.note: Bring about means cause a situation to happen; it is stronger than merely discussing peace.

items.example: The two delegations met to negotiate a peace agreement.
items.note: Negotiate means discuss terms in order to reach an agreed settlement.

items.example: The two sides called a truce to allow civilians to leave.
items.note: A truce is a temporary agreement to stop fighting; call means announce or agree to it.

items.example: Both sides called a ceasefire before the next round of talks.
items.note: A ceasefire is an agreement or order to stop shooting, often while negotiations continue.

items.example: The aid convoy will enter the area once a ceasefire is called.
items.note: Passive form often used in news reporting when the parties declaring it are not foregrounded.

items.example: Representatives signed a peace treaty at the end of the negotiations.
items.note: A treaty is a formal agreement, generally between states or other political authorities.

items.example: Both communities hoped the agreement would lead to lasting peace.
items.note: Lasting means continuing for a long period rather than ending soon.

items.example: A peace activist spoke at the event against violence.
items.note: A peace activist publicly works or campaigns to promote peace.

items.pt: manter a paz; preservar a ordem
items.example: Local observers tried to keep the peace after the demonstrations.
items.note: Means prevent fresh violence or disorder; it is different from bring about peace after conflict.

items.example: Officials worked with local leaders to restore order after the unrest.
items.note: Restore means return to an earlier state of order following disruption.

items.example: Peace negotiations resumed after a short interruption.
items.note: Refers to talks between parties aimed at ending or preventing conflict.

items.pt: as esperanças de paz diminuem; a esperança de paz se enfraquece
items.example: Hopes for peace faded when both sides rejected the proposal.
items.note: Fade means gradually weaken; it commonly combines with hopes or prospects.

items.pt: travar uma disputa contínua; enfrentar confrontos sucessivos
items.section: C · War expressions in everyday language
items.example: Residents fought a running battle with the council over noisy construction work.
items.note: A figurative expression for repeated conflict; unlike an actual battle, the dispute may be entirely nonviolent.

items.pt: resistir bravamente; lutar de maneira heroica
items.section: C · War expressions in everyday language
items.example: The small charity put up a heroic fight to keep the library open.
items.note: Put up a fight means resist or struggle; heroic adds admiration for exceptional courage or effort.

items.pt: perder a batalha; fracassar em uma disputa
items.section: C · War expressions in everyday language
items.example: The campaigners lost the battle to save the old building.
items.note: Can describe losing a literal battle or an effort to achieve a goal.

items.section: C · War expressions in everyday language
items.example: The protesters offered no resistance when asked to leave the road.
items.note: Offer resistance is more formal than resist; no means there was none.

items.section: C · War expressions in everyday language
items.example: The seriously injured climber fought for his life in hospital.
items.note: Used for someone struggling to survive a life-threatening condition, not necessarily in a military setting.

items.pt: guerra de preços; concorrência agressiva por preços
items.section: D · Figurative uses and exercise-supported collocations
items.example: A price war began when both supermarkets offered deeper discounts.
items.note: Figurative use of war for intense commercial competition.

items.pt: campanha de combate à criminalidade; guerra contra o crime
items.section: D · Figurative uses and exercise-supported collocations
items.example: The mayor announced a war on crime in the fictional city.
items.note: Figurative policy slogan; war here does not necessarily mean military action.

items.pt: travar uma luta contra a pobreza; combater a pobreza
items.section: D · Figurative uses and exercise-supported collocations
items.example: The charity argues that communities need long-term support to fight a war against poverty.
items.note: Metaphorical expression for sustained efforts against a social problem.

items.section: D · Figurative uses and exercise-supported collocations
items.example: The book describes a fierce battle near the river.
items.note: Fierce can modify both battle and fighting to stress intensity.

items.section: D · Figurative uses and exercise-supported collocations
items.example: The commander won a battle but failed to end the conflict.
items.note: Win is the conventional verb for success in a battle, literal or figurative.

items.section: D · Figurative uses and exercise-supported collocations
items.example: Volunteers helped a wounded soldier reach the medical centre.
items.note: Wounded relates to an injury, often caused by weapons or violence.

items.section: D · Figurative uses and exercise-supported collocations
items.example: The neighbouring states organised a peace conference for regional leaders.
items.note: A conference devoted to negotiating or promoting peace.
